The heavy reference stands in for the top model on every call
Fixed six-site design: ~4.37–4.57M users’ workload per datacenter
bubbles.unit: people targeted · fixed-campus capacity is lower
bubbles.assumption: 20 questions + 5 agent tasks per person daily. Peak rates: 4.6 output and 40 new input tokens/s per user. The heavy reference stands in for the top model.

bubbles.name: 1. SEED House
bubbles.headline: We rate the work, not the building
bullets: Score: people served per megawatt of power
Plus the carbon and water each person costs
Wood where people work; steel where computers run
bubbles.unit: users’ assumed workload per MW · illustrative
bubbles.assumption: Same daily workload and heavy-model proxy; source peak rates, before reliability reserves and context bottlenecks.

card.title: SEED House
card.what: a two-story mass-timber operations building (glulam and cross-laminated timber) with a green sedum roof.
card.why: timber stores carbon and cuts embodied carbon where people work. Insurers want the data halls noncombustible, so the timber goes here.
card.how: the campus is run from here. SEED rates the work, not the building: users served per megawatt, and the carbon and water each user costs.
math: ~4.37–4.57M users’ workload ÷ ~83.3 MW ≈ 52,000–55,000 users per MW.
This is a population capacity estimate at the assumed peak rates, not a count of simultaneous conversations. Carbon and water per user need a validated operating schedule.

bubbles.why: timber stores carbon and cuts embodied carbon where people work. Insurers want the data halls noncombustible, so the timber goes here.

bubbles.name: 2. Solar
bubbles.headline: Sun on every roof cuts what we buy
bullets: Panels on roofs, parking shades and the meadow
Inside our 500 MW limit: no extra computers
Small but real, and every bit helps
bubbles.assumption: …panels average ~14% of their rated output, the Massachusetts norm

card.title: Solar
card.what: about 3.3 MW of panels on the hall roof and parking canopies, plus about 2–3 MW over the borehole meadow.
card.why: every bit helps. Everything stays inside the 500 MW cap, so solar doesn't add chips; it cuts the energy we buy from the grid, and with it cost and carbon.
card.how: in Massachusetts, panels average about 14% of their rated output (17% of their inverter rating, per US energy data), so this is roughly 1% of the site's power. The rest is clean power bought from the grid.
math: 3.3 MW of roof and canopy panels × ~14% + 2–3 MW of meadow (inverter rating) × 17% ≈ 0.8–1.0 MW, about 1% of the site's 83 MW, or ~7–9 GWh a year not bought from the grid.
Meadow: 260 × 250 m ≈ 16 acres, at about 5.5–7.6 acres per MW (NREL) ≈ 2–3 MW.

bubbles.why: every bit helps. Everything stays inside the 500 MW cap, so solar doesn't add chips; it cuts the energy we buy from the grid, and with it cost and carbon.

bubbles.name: 3. Inside a data hall
bubbles.headline: Water, not air, cools the chips
bullets: 368 rack positions drawn; 338 active rack pairs fit the midpoint power allowance
Each rack makes ~5× the heat air can carry
Sealed rooms: muggy, salty outside air stays out
bubbles.unit: per compute rack + 14 kW for networking and storage
bubbles.assumption: 210 kW is the midpoint of the reported 190–230 kW range. The drawing uses the lower end; operating capacity uses 338 pairs.

card.title: Inside a sealed data hall
card.what: NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 racks (72 GPUs each, 190–230 kW), fully liquid-cooled, in sealed, vapor-tight halls.
card.why: air-cooled racks top out near 40 kW (NVIDIA's guidance), and these draw ~190–230 kW. Sealing keeps muggy summer air, dry winter air and salt outside.
card.how: cold plates on every chip pass the heat into water, which goes in at up to 113°F (45°C) and comes out at about 131°F (55°C). Networking racks get rear-door coils, pushed by their own fans. The water never drops below 77°F (25°C), well above the hall air's dew point (kept under 50°F, 10°C), so nothing condenses on the pipes or chips.
math: At the midpoint: 338 × (210 + 14) kW × 1.10 ≈ 83.28 MW per campus; 338 × 72 = 24,336 active GPUs. The 368 drawn positions would use ~90.7 MW at this midpoint, so they cannot all run at that draw within the allowance.

Water out: NVIDIA says coolant entering a Rubin chip at 113°F (45°C) leaves at about 131°F (55°C). Lenovo's flow table for the earlier GB300 rack gives ~131°F (55°C) out at every inlet from 77 to 113°F (25–45°C), so we assume the same for Rubin (our estimate).
More calls, longer outputs and input reprocessing use more chip time. With fixed hardware and power, fewer users’ workload fits.

bubbles.referenceAssumption: The heavy reference stands in for the top model. Peak sizing uses 4.6 output + 40 new input tokens/s per user; hardware transfer and cache behavior still need validation.
bubbles.why: air-cooled racks top out near 40 kW (NVIDIA's guidance), and these draw ~190–230 kW. Sealing keeps muggy summer air, dry winter air and salt outside.

bubbles.name: 4. Service spine
bubbles.headline: Warm water is cool enough
bullets: The racks accept water up to 113°F (45°C)
So our water floats with the weather: 70–106°F (21–41°C)
Warm water can be cooled by plain outdoor air

card.title: Service spine
card.what: cooling units and pumps along the hall's north side, one cooling unit at the end of each row, with pipes to the racks in covered floor trenches.
card.why: it's one short run from every hall to the coolers, it keeps pipes out of the electrical rooms, and no cooling pipe runs over a rack, as insurers require.
card.how: the units pass heat from the rack loop to the building loop. That water floats between 70 and 106°F (21–41°C) with the weather and returns at about 124°F (51°C).
math: Rack inlet ≤ 113°F (45°C), minus ~7°F (4°C) across the cooling units, means building water ≤ 106°F (41°C).
Return: the racks' ~131°F (55°C) − 7°F ≈ 124°F (51°C).

bubbles.why: it's one short run from every hall to the coolers, it keeps pipes out of the electrical rooms, and no cooling pipe runs over a rack, as insurers require.

bubbles.name: 5. Cooling ridge
bubbles.headline: Outdoor air does the cooling, no water used
bullets: 102 giant radiators with fans, on a raised deck
Sealed coils: no water evaporates, no cooling towers
No chillers needed for the chips
bubbles.assumption: …a typical weather year; a hot summer needs ~20 hours of help

card.title: Cooling ridge
card.what: 102 dry coolers on short legs on a 6 m steel deck, fed by three pipe bridges. No cooling towers, and no chillers for the chips.
card.why: dry coolers use no water, and warm-water chips let outdoor air do all the cooling in all but one hour of a typical year.
card.how: fans pull outside air up through finned coils. The fluid inside is water mixed with Dow's DOWFROST antifreeze (an inhibited propylene glycol), so in normal running it never gets colder than the high teens °F, and it stays liquid down to about 2°F (−16°C). About 73 coolers serve the chips and 29 the room air. The deck and legs keep snow clear. In winter the fans slow, coolers switch off, and a bypass valve keeps the building's water at 70°F (21°C) or warmer. In a long winter outage, the coolers are closed off and drained into indoor tanks.
math: Coolers bring water within ~9°F (5°C) of the outside air, so 106°F (41°C) water works up to 97°F (36°C) outdoors. Cambridge's hottest hour (Boston-Logan weather file, 2011–2025) is 97°F (36.1°C): 1 hour in 8,760.
Cooler fans use about 0.2% of the site's energy a year.

bubbles.why: dry coolers use no water, and warm-water chips let outdoor air do all the cooling in all but one hour of a typical year.

bubbles.name: 6. Geothermal cooling
bubbles.headline: Room air: the ground first, then chillers
bullets: About 1,000 holes, 150 m (500 ft) deep
Winter air chills the rock; summer heat goes back in
Six air-cooled chillers stand by for heat waves
bubbles.assumption: …the rock behaves like typical local granite; a test bore confirms it before drilling

card.title: Geothermal cooling
card.what: about 1,000 boreholes, 150 m deep under the meadow, run from the Cold Battery House, with six air-cooled chillers as backup.
card.why: on warm days outdoor air can't make the 75°F (24°C) water the room-air loop needs. The ground does it with only pumps running, using less power than chillers every year; the chillers are insurance.
card.how: in winter the same coolers chill the rock; in summer heat goes back into it. This is geothermal cooling, not power: rock hot enough for power is 4–6 miles down here.
math: Room-air heat: networking racks (~14 kW per compute rack, 4.3–5.1 MW) + electrical losses (1–3% of 75 MW) ≈ 5–7 MW.
Coolers make 75°F (24°C) water only when it's below 66°F (19°C) outside. In Cambridge it's warmer than that ~2,290 hours a year, and the ground covers those hours.
An hour-by-hour model needs ~950 boreholes (~1,050 in a hot summer, with the chillers covering the gap), so we drill ~1,000.
Against chillers alone, the field saves ~650–1,130 MWh a year and 1.1–1.7 MW at the hottest hour per site (preliminary model outputs).

bubbles.why: on warm days outdoor air can't make the 75°F (24°C) water the room-air loop needs. The ground does it with only pumps running, using less power than chillers every year; the chillers are insurance.

bubbles.name: 7. Greenhouse
bubbles.headline: Waste heat warms a greenhouse
bullets: Warm water leaving the halls heats the glass house
At full IT load, ~75 MW becomes heat; the greenhouse needs well under 1 MW
Heat is a resource, not just waste
bubbles.unit: warm return-water design point · availability varies with load
bubbles.assumption: ~300 W/m² peak greenhouse demand, roughly estimated. Recoverable heat follows IT load; off-peak backup heat is not sized.

card.title: Greenhouse
card.what: a glass greenhouse heated by the datacenter.
card.why: it puts waste heat to use instead of sending it all into the air.
card.how: Warm return water is designed around 124°F (51°C). Its usable heat output depends on the computers’ load; the workload assumption does not establish round-the-clock heat availability.
math: At modeled full load, the campus IT demand is ~75 MW and becomes heat. The 60 × 30 m greenhouse needs roughly 1,800 m² × 300 W/m² = 0.54 MW at peak. Heat recovered by this particular circuit and off-peak backup must still be engineered.

bubbles.why: it puts waste heat to use instead of sending it all into the air.

bubbles.name: 8. Substation and grid
bubbles.headline: The datacenter keeps its power limit
bullets: About 83.3 MW per datacenter; 500 MW across six sites
More AI work per person reduces capacity, not the power limit
User sessions can pause while other users keep the machines busy
bubbles.assumption: 338 active rack pairs per site, 210 + 14 kW each, PUE 1.10; before a solar credit.

card.title: Substation and grid
card.what: a ~83 MW grid connection (one-sixth of the 500 MW fleet), with clean power bought through contracts with new clean power plants.
card.why: the challenge caps grid power. Massachusetts has no geothermal power plants and only modest sun, so clean power is bought, not made. The state's new rules for big datacenters (Executive Order 658, September 2026) ask for exactly this: new clean generation to match what we use.
card.how: a 115,000-volt line comes in from the east and transformers step it down.
math: 338 × 224 kW × 1.10 = 83.2832 MW at modeled full load. Six sites total 499.6992 MW.
At 83.28 MW, one hour at full load uses 83.28 MWh. Actual daily and annual energy depend on the load over time.
Peak token rates size the hardware. They are not assumed to run continuously for eight or 24 hours, and no shift or quota-wait multiplier is added.

bubbles.why: the challenge caps grid power. Massachusetts has no geothermal power plants and only modest sun, so clean power is bought, not made. The state's new rules for big datacenters (Executive Order 658, September 2026) ask for exactly this: new clean generation to match what we use.
bubbles.referenceAssumption: The heavy reference stands in for the top model. Peak sizing uses 4.6 output + 40 new input tokens/s per user; hardware transfer and cache behavior still need validation.

bubbles.name: 9. Backup power
bubbles.headline: Proven backup, on cleaner fuel
bullets: Batteries carry the first minutes, cooling pumps included
Then ~30 generators run on renewable diesel
48 hours of fuel on site; deliveries after that
bubbles.unit: less carbon over the fuel's life
bubbles.assumption: …certified waste-oil fuel; soy-based fuel saves less (~47%)
bubbles.source: calc 16 · Kao Data · California fuel data

card.title: Backup power
card.what: batteries for the first minutes, then standard generators running on renewable diesel, with room to add hydrogen fuel cells later.
card.why: it's proven and insurable, and Kao Data has run its UK campus this way since 2021. Renewable diesel cuts the generators' lifetime fuel carbon by 50–80%, and they only run for tests and rare outages, so backup fuel is under 1% of the site's footprint.
card.how: if the grid drops, batteries carry the load for minutes while about 30 generators start. 48 hours of fuel sits in four tanks, and deliveries keep them running in longer outages.
math: Fuel for the existing full campus: 48 h × ~82 MW × ~0.28 L/kWh ≈ 1.1 million litres. Fewer users do not shrink the backup requirement for a fully loaded campus.
Kao Data's Harlow campus plans "more than 750,000 litres" of HVO for 35–71 MW of IT.
Carbon: 20 test hours a year ≈ 0.2 million litres ≈ 510–570 t CO₂ on diesel, ~100–290 t on renewable diesel, against ~86,000–97,000 t for a year of grid power at New England's 2024 mix.

bubbles.why: it's proven and insurable, and Kao Data has run its UK campus this way since 2021. Renewable diesel cuts the generators' lifetime fuel carbon by 50–80%, and they only run for tests and rare outages, so backup fuel is under 1% of the site's footprint.

bubbles.name: 10. The whole campus
bubbles.headline: How many people fit in one datacenter?
bullets: Same workload: 20 questions and five agent tasks per person daily
Six sites support ~26.2–27.4 million users’ assumed workload
The heavy reference handles every call; the 500 MW limit stays fixed
bubbles.assumption: 4.6 output + 40 new input tokens/s per source user at peak; efficient context reuse; no reliability or latency reserve included.

card.title: The same workload within a fixed campus
card.what: Same workload: 20 questions and five agent tasks per person daily
card.why: The hardware supports the population whose assumed peak workload fits. The daily task count is unchanged; the heavy model uses more chip time, so fewer users fit within the fixed power limit.
card.how: Each agent task may make several calls. The source workload already includes questions and agent tasks in its 4.6 output and 40 new input tokens/s peak rates. Do not multiply those rates by the task count again.
math: 338 rack pairs × (210 + 14) kW × 1.10 = 83.28 MW per campus.
Peak work per source user: 4.6 output + 40 new input ÷ 10 = 8.6 output-equivalent tokens/s.

Six equal sites support ~26.2–27.4 million users’ workload, about 6.55–6.85% of the 400M target.

bullets: 338 compute racks per datacenter; 2,028 across six sites

The heavy model still lowers the people served for the same workload

hall.name: Main hall
hall.text: A one-story steel hall with stone-wool walls that can't burn, as insurers require. The low roof keeps the coolers' tops above it, so they breathe freely.

roofSolar.name: Roof solar
roofSolar.text: Panels on the hall roof. They count inside our 500 megawatt (MW) limit, so they cut the power we buy rather than adding computers.

sealed.name: Sealed data hall
sealed.text: Outside air never comes in. Boston-area air has the right humidity for computers only 69% of the year, so we cool through water instead.

compute.name: Compute rack
compute.text: An NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack: 72 AI chips (GPUs), cooled by water through metal plates on every chip. Water goes in at up to 113°F (45°C) and comes out at about 131°F (55°C). Operational sizing uses 338 compute racks plus their support allowance. More AI work per person reduces how many users these racks can serve.
compute.number: 368 positions drawn; 338 active rack pairs per campus at midpoint power

network.name: Networking and storage rack with rear-door coil
network.text: It holds the network switches and the flash drives that remember each user's conversations. Its own fans push warm air through a water coil on its back door, so the heat goes straight to water.

trench.name: Floor pipe trench
trench.text: Cooling pipes run in covered trenches in the floor, never over the racks, as insurers now require. A leak drains into a lined trench with a sensing cable, and power cables run overhead, away from water.
trench.number: no pipe joints above any rack

fire.name: Sprinklers and smoke sampling
fire.text: Wet-pipe sprinklers: always full of water, the safest choice for people. Thin pipes draw air to very sensitive smoke detectors, so alarms sound before smoke builds.
fire.number: ~500 gallons a minute where a fire starts

spine.name: Service spine and cooling units
spine.text: Cooling units at the end of each row pass the racks' heat to the building's water. That water floats between 70 and 106°F (21–41°C) with the weather.

electrical.name: Electrical rooms and batteries
electrical.text: Batteries carry the computers *and* the cooling pumps until the generators start. If the pumps stopped, the chip water would warm about 4°F (2.4°C) a minute.

bridges.name: Pipe bridges
bridges.text: They carry the warm chip loop and the cooler room-air loop between the hall and the cooling ridge. Outside the halls, the loops carry Dow's DOWFROST antifreeze.

coolers.name: Dry coolers
coolers.text: Giant radiators with fans. Outdoor air cools the chip loop through sealed coils, so nothing evaporates, and the chips never need chillers in a typical year. The fluid is water mixed with Dow's DOWFROST antifreeze: in normal running it never gets colder than the high teens °F, and it stays liquid down to about 2°F (−16°C).

chillers.name: Backup chillers
chillers.text: Air conditioners for water. Six stand by to cool the room-air water in heat waves or when the borehole field is serviced. They use no water.

boreholes.name: Borehole field
boreholes.text: About 1,000 holes, 500 ft (150 m) deep. Winter air chills the rock; on warm days the rock takes the room air's heat with only pumps running. This is geothermal cooling, not power.

batteryHouse.name: Cold Battery House
batteryHouse.text: The pumps and pipes that run the borehole field. It's timber-clad, with a green roof.

solar.name: Meadow and parking-canopy solar
solar.text: More panels over the meadow and the parking. With the roof they make about 1% of the site's power.

substation.name: Substation
substation.text: Where the site connects to the grid: about 83 MW from a 115,000-volt line. We buy clean power through contracts with new clean power plants.

generators.name: Generator yard
generators.text: About 30 standard generators running on renewable diesel, made from fats and oils (we require waste sources). Cleaner engines keep smog-forming exhaust low. It isn't zero-emission, but it cuts the fuel's lifetime carbon by 50–80%.

fuel.name: Fuel tanks
fuel.text: Two days (48 hours) of renewable diesel on site, with a delivery contract for longer outages.

reserved.name: Reserved fuel-cell pad
reserved.text: Space kept for hydrogen fuel cells once they're proven at this scale. Today they would cost far more.

house.name: SEED House
house.text: The operations building, and the one place we use mass timber, which stores carbon.

greenhouse.name: Waste-heat greenhouse
greenhouse.text: Warm return water can heat it on the way to the coolers. Available heat follows IT load; off-peak backup heat remains to be sized.

snowpad.name: Snow storage pad
snowpad.text: Plowed snow goes here, away from the coolers' air intakes and the wetlands.

dewpoint.name: Dew point sensors
dewpoint.text: They measure how damp the hall air is. A surface warmer than the air's "dew point" stays dry, so we keep the dew point under 50°F (10°C) and the water at least ~27°F warmer. Nothing "sweats" like a cold glass on a summer day.
dewpoint.number: water never below 77°F (25°C) at the racks

freshAir.name: Fresh-air unit
freshAir.text: It brings in the small amount of fresh air staff need and keeps the halls at slightly higher pressure, so any leak blows dry air out instead of letting damp air in. A cold coil wrings the moisture out of that air first.
freshAir.number: hall air drier than a 50°F (10°C) dew point

airlock.name: Loading-dock airlock and staging
airlock.text: Two doors with a space between them, never open together, so damp or icy outdoor air stays out. New racks rest here for a few hours to warm up, so they don't fog up like a cold bottle brought indoors.
airlock.number: 3 dock doors, each with an airlock

bypass.name: Bypass valve
bypass.text: In cold weather, outdoor air could chill the water far too much. Like a car's thermostat, this valve sends some warm water around the coolers, so the building's water never drops below 70°F (21°C).

freezeProtection.name: Cooler valves, drain lines and freeze sensors
freezeProtection.text: Each cooler has a freeze sensor and its own shut-off and drain valves. If a long winter power outage stops the heat, the coolers are closed off and drained into indoor tanks, while the pumps keep running on backup power.
freezeProtection.number: pumps need under 1 MW of backup

drainTanks.name: Drain-down tanks
drainTanks.text: Indoor tanks that catch the coolers' fluid in a winter outage. Any fluid left in a cooler turns to slush, not ice, so pipes and coils don't burst; it thaws before cooling restarts.

coldInsulation.name: Insulated cold pipes
coldInsulation.text: In winter the ground loop runs as cold as about 19°F (−7°C). Its pipes wear thick insulation with a sealed jacket, so damp air can't reach the cold metal and drip.

scope.title: The same daily workload within fixed campuses
scope.why: SEED means Sustainable, Energy-Efficient Datacenters. We keep each datacenter’s power fixed and calculate how much of the original 400-million-person workload fits when every call uses the heavy reference.
scope.html:
The challenge targets 400 million people, six sites, 500 MW and $30B over five years. We keep the physical limits and report how much of that population’s assumed workload fits.

Each person has 20 questions and five agent tasks daily. A task may make several AI calls. The heavy reference stands in for the top model on every call.

The supplied case C peak rates remain 4.6 output and 40 new input tokens/s per source user. They are peak sizing inputs, not continuous daily generation rates.

No active-hour schedule, daily-cohort multiplier or extra concurrency discount is assumed. Land, grid access and rock testing remain unresolved.

Per-campus power allowance
~83.3 MW
Daily workload
20 questions + 5 agent tasks per person
Capacity per campus
~4.37–4.57M users’ workload, illustrative
scope.notes: Planning basis20 questions and five agent tasks per person daily, with the heavy reference for the top model. Source peak rates, hardware transfer and cache behavior determine the estimate; this is not measured Claude performance.Original input referencescalc 01, power to the chips

power.title: Buy clean power; make what the site allows
power.html:
What we chose

Clean power bought over the grid through long-term contracts for new clean plants. About 5.8 MW of solar panels per site on the roof, parking canopies and meadow, counted inside the 500 MW cap. And little is wasted: SEED's design allowance for power usage effectiveness (PUE, the site's total power divided by its computers' power) is 1.1, and the cooling model suggests 1.03–1.07.

Why

The challenge caps grid power, and Massachusetts can't make clean power at this scale on a campus. It has no geothermal power plants: rock hot enough for power, about 300°F (150°C), starts about 4 miles down and is mostly 4.5–6 miles down (MIT, 2006). Solar averages about 17% of its inverter (AC) rating (EIA, 2024) and about 14% of its panels' (DC) rating, so it only trims what we buy.

Contracts that pay for new plants are how large operators "make" clean power, and a new state order calls for them. Governor Healey's Executive Order 658 (8 Sep 2026) says projects over 25 MW must sign a community benefits agreement and buy "incremental new" clean power, eligible under the state's Clean Energy Standard, to match their yearly use, or pay into a Ratepayer Protection Fund. Existing hydro likely won't count. The output of New England Clean Energy Connect (NECEC), the new line from Québec, is already under 20-year contracts to Massachusetts utilities, so SEED doesn't plan to buy it.

Every watt saved on cooling goes to chips. At PUE 1.1, 455 of the 500 MW reaches the computers. A typical large site, at 1.44 (the Uptime Institute's 2025 average for sites of 20 MW and up), gets 347 MW. So SEED makes 31% more IT power available under the same cap, or 40% more against the all-site average of 1.54.

Numbers

Energy at 500 MW, a year
4.4 TWh
Share of Massachusetts sales
~9%
Solar, average per site
0.8–1.0 MW
Budgeted price
10–18.2¢/kWh
Industry PUE, all sites / 20 MW and up
1.54 / 1.44
More IT power under the cap than at PUE 1.44
31%

Fixed-workload correction: 20 questions and five agent tasks per person daily, with the heavy reference for the top model. About 83.3 MW per site and 500 MW across six sites remain fixed. The resulting capacity is ~4.37–4.57M users’ workload per site at the source peak rates.
power.why:
The challenge caps grid power, and Massachusetts can't make clean power at this scale on a campus. It has no geothermal power plants: rock hot enough for power, about 300°F (150°C), starts about 4 miles down and is mostly 4.5–6 miles down (MIT, 2006). Solar averages about 17% of its inverter (AC) rating (EIA, 2024) and about 14% of its panels' (DC) rating, so it only trims what we buy.

Contracts that pay for new plants are how large operators "make" clean power, and a new state order calls for them. Governor Healey's Executive Order 658 (8 Sep 2026) says projects over 25 MW must sign a community benefits agreement and buy "incremental new" clean power, eligible under the state's Clean Energy Standard, to match their yearly use, or pay into a Ratepayer Protection Fund. Existing hydro likely won't count. The output of New England Clean Energy Connect (NECEC), the new line from Québec, is already under 20-year contracts to Massachusetts utilities, so SEED doesn't plan to buy it.

Every watt saved on cooling goes to chips. At PUE 1.1, 455 of the 500 MW reaches the computers. A typical large site, at 1.44 (the Uptime Institute's 2025 average for sites of 20 MW and up), gets 347 MW. So SEED makes 31% more IT power available under the same cap, or 40% more against the all-site average of 1.54.
power.notes: Set asideMaking the bulk on site: 40 MW of average solar alone needs ~1,200–1,900 acres plus storage. Small reactors and deep geothermal power: after 2030, so space can be reserved.SourcesEIA Massachusetts electricity profile (2024 sales; solar at 17% of inverter rating) · EIA Electric Power Annual, Table 2.10 (18.2¢ industrial price, 5th highest) · MIT, The Future of Geothermal Energy (2006, Table A.2.1) · Executive Order 658 (archived copy) · Avangrid's NECEC release (16 Jan 2026, hosted by WBUR) · Uptime Institute 2025 survey (PUE) · NREL solar land-use report (2013, acres per MW)Mathcalc 01 · calc 14 · calc 15

computers.title: 338 active rack pairs per datacenter
computers.why: air-cooled racks top out near 40 kW (NVIDIA's guidance), and these draw ~190–230 kW. Sealing keeps muggy summer air, dry winter air and salt outside.
computers.html:
The design still has 368 drawn rack positions. At the 210 kW midpoint plus 14 kW support and PUE 1.10, 338 active pairs fit each 83.3 MW allowance. At the lower 190 kW compute draw, all 368 positions fit.

Six independently capped campuses therefore operate 2,028 pairs. We cannot pool the small leftover power between sites to activate a 2,029th pair.

The capacity calculation uses 72 GPUs per rack and an assumed 2.5× rack throughput gain over the GB300 heavy-reference benchmark. Applying the R1 hardware gain to Llama and this workload needs validation.

No capacity reserve is included. Additional context storage, attention work, memory bandwidth, maintenance and latency requirements can lower the usable headcount.

models.why: The hardware supports the population whose assumed peak workload fits. The daily task count is unchanged; the heavy model uses more chip time, so fewer users fit within the fixed power limit.

The same daily workload is retained. Every question and every call within an agent task uses the heavy reference; there is no weaker-model routing.

memory.title: An agent task can involve many AI calls
memory.why: The daily task count is not a count of model calls. Context, tool results and repeated processing also consume computing resources.
memory.html:
The daily workload is 20 questions plus five agent tasks per person. Each task can involve several AI calls; code, conversation history and tool results can be processed again on later calls.

The case C source lists 104 million context reads per person per day, separately from the 40 new input tokens/s peak rate. Repeated reads are not the same as new input, stored data or network downloads.

The baseline assumes effective context reuse. Cache hits still require attention, memory and bandwidth; misses require additional input processing.

Cache size, bandwidth and added support power remain unvalidated. The old R1-specific 2.3 EB and flash-cost estimates do not size the chosen heavy model. Peak rates alone do not establish daily token totals.

chip-loop.title: Warm water and dry coolers
chip-loop.html:
What we chose

Cold plates on every chip. Water goes in at up to 113°F (45°C) and comes out at about 131°F (55°C), NVIDIA's figures for its fully liquid-cooled Rubin chips. Coolant distribution units (CDUs) link the racks' loops to the building's water, which runs about 7°F (4°C) cooler. That water floats between 70 and 106°F (21–41°C) with the weather and runs to 102 dry coolers (73 for the chips) on a 6 m deck. Each cooler stands on ~1.3 m legs, so it clears the settled snow by at least 2 ft, bracing included (the US loads standard ASCE 7-16, §7.8, per O'Rourke's guide). Backup chillers trim the rare shortfall.

Why

Because the racks accept warm water, up to 113°F (45°C) in NVIDIA's Vera Rubin design and Lenovo's GB300 guide, outdoor air alone can cool the chips in 8,759 of 8,760 hours in Cambridge, with no chillers and no water evaporated. Fixed cold water would need chillers and use about 2.7× the energy.

Water at 70–77°F (21–25°C)
63% of hours
Fans + pumps a year, per site
~1,580 MWh
Fixed 90°F (32°C) + chillers instead
~4,250 MWh
Hot summer, +3.6°F (+2°C)
20 h trimmed
Step across the CDUs
~7°F (4°C)

room-air.title: The ground first, chillers as backup
room-air.html:
What we chose

Rear-door water coils on the networking racks and fan coils in the electrical rooms, on a 75°F (24°C) loop. Dry coolers handle it below ~66°F (19°C) outdoors. On warm hours, about 1,000 boreholes, 150 m deep under the meadow, take the heat with only pumps running; winter air recharges the rock. Six warm-water air-cooled chillers of ~1.7 MW each stand by: 10 MW per site, five to carry the room air and one spare. The example unit is Johnson Controls' YVAM class, which makes 59–86°F (15–30°C) water.

Changed 18 Oct after the source check; confirmed by Arturo. It was four chillers of ~2.5 MW, but no unit that size exists in these product lines. The chiller we first named, Trane's Ascend ACR, tops out at ~2 MW and makes water no warmer than 68–72°F (20–22°C), so it can't make our 75°F (24°C) water directly.

The coils keep the halls inside the recommended range of ASHRAE, the heating and cooling engineers' society: 64–81°F (18–27°C), with a dew point of 16 to 59°F (−9 to 15°C). Relative humidity may reach 70% only if corrosion test strips (coupons) pass; otherwise it stays at 50% or below.

Why

Outdoor air can't make 75°F (24°C) water for about 2,290 hours a year. The ground does it with less power than chillers every year and keeps SEED passive. The chillers are insurance if the rock, the share of heat in the air, or the summer is worse than modeled. Arturo chose this over a chillers-only design: it doesn't pay back on electricity alone, but it uses less power over time.

At 95°F (35°C) outdoors, making 68°F (20°C) water, the chillers give about 4.4–4.6 units of cooling per unit of power (Vertiv's Liebert AFC datasheet). About 6 at 75°F (24°C) water in milder hours is our estimate; the model is also tested at 4.

sealed.title: Sealed halls: outside air never comes in
sealed.html:
What we chose

Vapor-tight, slightly pressurized data halls. Only a small, dried stream of fresh air comes in for staff. Every outdoor coil, on the coolers and chillers alike, touches outside air only on its outside.

Why

Cambridge's air is cool enough 94% of the year but has the right humidity only 69% of the time. Muggy summer air, dry winter air, salt, smoke and pollen all stay outside.

fluid.title: 35% glycol outdoors, 25% in the racks
fluid.html:
What we chose

Dow's DOWFROST, an inhibited propylene glycol, at about 35% propylene glycol by weight (about 36% DOWFROST) in the building, outdoor and borehole loops. The racks' own loops stay on PG25, a premixed 25% propylene glycol coolant. The ground stops recharging below 14°F (−10°C) outdoors, which keeps the running fluid out of the deepest cold.

Why

In normal running the fluid never gets colder than the high teens °F (about −7°C), and it stays liquid down to about 2°F (−16°C). It was sized for colder inland Holyoke, where the 50-year low is −28°F (−33°C); Cambridge's is −13°F (−24.8°C), so there's extra margin. Even if the pumps stopped in a deep freeze, it would turn to slush rather than split the pipes, by Dow's tables. Stronger mixes would make the pumps work harder all year.

Numbers (Dow)

Coldest running fluid
high teens °F (−7°C)
Stays liquid down to
~2°F (−16°C)

hall.title: A low steel hall that can't burn
hall.html:
What we chose

A 210 × 60 m one-story steel hall (recycled steel) on a low-carbon concrete slab, with a low roof (8–9.5 m) carrying solar, stone-wool-core metal wall panels and wood-look noncombustible cladding.

Cooling pipes stay below the racks. The coolant distribution units (CDUs) stand at the row ends along the hall's edge. Noncombustible pipes (stainless steel, welded where possible, no push-fit joints) run in covered trenches in the floor slab under the aisles, over noncombustible drip containment, with quick disconnects only at each rack's manifold. Power busway and cable trays stay overhead, so nothing wet sits above the racks or the power.

Changed 18 Oct after the source check; confirmed by Arturo. The pipes ran overhead, in a drip-panned tray beside the power lines. FM Global's data-center data sheet (DS 5-32, January 2026 edition) bars cooling pipes above critical equipment (§2.2.1.6), wants them below the room or along its edge with no joints over equipment (§2.5.2.10–2.5.2.12), and asks for noncombustible pipe, preferably welded (§2.5.2.4–2.5.2.5).

Why

Insurers require noncombustible data halls (FM Global DS 5-32, §2.2.1.1), and stone wool doesn't burn. The low roof keeps the cooler tops (~9.9 m) above it so they breathe freely, as Evapco's layout guide asks, which matters because hot-day winds blow from the west and southwest across the hall toward the coolers.

Timber would save less carbon here than in Microsoft's two timber-hybrid datacenters (35% less embodied carbon than steel, by Microsoft's estimate, with no method stated). Their saving came from replacing elevated concrete floors; a one-story hall on a slab would save mainly on the roof (WoodWorks, p.31). And civil, structural and architectural work is only ~30% of a datacenter's upfront embodied carbon, servers excluded (Arup), so timber could cut the whole building's by ~10% at most (our estimate). So the hall uses low-carbon concrete and recycled steel, and timber goes where people work.

house.title: Timber where people work; waste heat for plants
house.html:
Revised operating assumption: Recoverable heat follows IT load. The workload scenario does not establish a continuous 75 MW heat supply or guaranteed return temperature. Off-peak backup heating remains to be sized.

What we chose

The SEED House, a two-story mass-timber operations building with a sedum roof, plus timber on the Cold Battery House and entry canopies. A 60 × 30 m glass greenhouse heated by the ~124°F (51°C) return water.

Why

Timber stores carbon and is welcome where people work, away from the data halls. The greenhouse puts a sliver of the waste heat to use instead of sending it all into the air.

Numbers

~0.5 MW
Total IT heat at full load
~75 MW

backup.title: Batteries, then generators on renewable diesel
backup.html:
What we chose

Batteries (an uninterruptible power supply, UPS) carry the computers, cooling pumps and controls for the first minutes. About 30 standard ~3 MW generators with the cleanest engines (EPA Tier 4 Final) take over, running on renewable diesel (hydrotreated vegetable oil, HVO), with 48 hours of fuel on site and a resupply contract. Space is reserved to add hydrogen fuel cells later.

Why

It's proven, insurable and already in a normal building's cost. Kao Data has run its UK campus's backup generators on HVO since 2021, and US operators are following (below). Engine makers approve it: Caterpillar and mtu as a drop-in fuel, and Kohler for all its mission-critical gensets with no changes (its US approval follows ASTM D975, the diesel standard). Cummins approves it in all its generator sets except some QSX15 configurations, and says to confirm with the supplier that the HVO suits all site temperatures.

HVO cuts lifecycle carbon by about 50–80% (our estimate from California's figures; its renewable diesel averaged ~58% below fossil diesel in Q2 2025), but it isn't zero-emission: it still has tailpipe emissions. Generators only run for tests and rare outages, so their fuel is under 1% of a site's footprint.

The full-campus concept stores about 1.1 million litres for 48 hours. Fewer users at the same loaded power do not reduce this backup requirement.

fire.title: Safest for people, and leaks that shut themselves off
fire.html:
What we chose

Wet-pipe sprinklers with quick-response heads at FM Global's baseline for every data hall, with or without batteries: 0.2 gallons per minute (gpm) per ft² over 2,500 ft², ~500 gpm (FM data sheet DS 5-32, 2026 edition, §2.4.3.3.1.1). Add FM's 250 gpm hose allowance and a 60-minute supply (§2.4.1.5–2.4.1.6): ~45,000 gallons (~170 m³) of fire water by our estimate, before the hydraulic design adds its margin. In rows with battery units, add 20-gauge steel side barriers every third rack (§2.4.3.6.1.1).

Changed 18 Oct after the source check; confirmed by Arturo. FM's January 2026 edition made this the baseline for every hall. The 2022 edition's lighter option for halls without batteries (0.1 gpm/ft² over 1,500 ft², ~150 gpm) is gone, so that comparison is dropped. The hose allowance, 60-minute supply and steel barriers are new.

Aspirating (air-sampling) smoke detectors for very early warning (§2.4.2.1.2), and no fire-suppression gas. Fire walls: 1-hour around each data hall and network room, and 2-hour between halls (§2.2.4.1–2.2.4.1.1). The rooms for the uninterruptible power supply (UPS) and batteries follow FM's data sheets DS 5-28 and DS 5-33, which we haven't checked yet.

Changed 18 Oct after the source check; for Arturo to confirm. It was 1-hour walls around halls and battery rooms, the 2022 edition's rule.

Leak sensors at NVIDIA's three levels (inside each compute tray, in each rack, and at the cooling units), plus our own at the rack manifolds, along the floor and along the pipe runs. They're FM Approved and addressable, and alarm to a constantly monitored building-management system (§2.5.2.14). Noncombustible drip containment sits under the liquid-cooled racks (§2.5.2.13), and the piping isolates a leak to one rack (§2.5.2.9), with automatic shutoff. The racks' coolant, PG25 (25% propylene glycol), meets FM's rule that coolant can't ignite (§2.5.2.1).

Changed 18 Oct after the source check; confirmed by Arturo. FM's 2026 edition (§2.5.2) sets the sensor, containment and one-rack isolation rules above. The pipes, which ran overhead in a drip-panned tray beside the power lines, now run in covered floor trenches (see Hall and materials).

Why

Arturo's rule: "whatever is safest for the people." FM ranks wet pipes first (§2.4.1.1–2.4.1.2): they're the most reliable and fastest. Early detection gets people out, and with no gas nobody works in a room designed to be flooded. Leaks matter too: in FM's 15-year loss study, liquids cause ~24% of datacenter loss costs (DS 5-32, Table 3.6.1-1), though ~9 points of that is sprinkler leakage, not coolant. So a leaking rack or row shuts itself down.

Batteries in the racks bring two sets of rules. FM's rack-battery rules cover up to 20 kWh per rack (§2.3.1.4.1); above that, the rack counts as an energy storage system under DS 5-33. And we assume NFPA 855, the National Fire Protection Association's standard for stationary batteries, covers halls with in-rack batteries unless the fire department exempts them, because its 20 kWh lithium threshold counts a whole fire area. Its default limit is 600 kWh per fire area, with more allowed after approval, a hazard analysis and testing. It calls for explosion control under NFPA 69 (NFPA's committee records) and large-scale fire testing (UL).

Leaks matter too: in FM's 15-year loss study, liquids cause ~24% of datacenter loss costs (DS 5-32, Table 3.6.1-1), though ~9 points of that is sprinkler leakage, not coolant. So a leaking rack or row shuts itself down.

Batteries in the racks bring two sets of rules. FM's rack-battery rules cover up to 20 kWh per rack (§2.3.1.4.1); above that, the rack counts as an energy storage system under DS 5-33. And we assume NFPA 855, the National Fire Protection Association's standard for stationary batteries, covers halls with in-rack batteries unless the fire department exempts them, because its 20 kWh lithium threshold counts a whole fire area. Its default limit is 600 kWh per fire area, with more allowed after approval, a hazard analysis and testing. It calls for explosion control under NFPA 69 (NFPA's committee records) and large-scale fire testing (UL).
fire.notes: Set asidePreaction sprinklers (dry pipes, but detectors must work first). Double-interlock preaction, which one panelist at a June 2026 industry roundtable called typical (Schlosser, Jensen Hughes), would need a 3,500 ft² dry-pipe design area (~700 gpm), and FM ranks it last (§2.4.1.1–2.4.1.2). Clean-agent and hybrid (water plus inert gas) systems: FM rules them out with lithium batteries in the racks (§2.4.3.6.4.1); without them, it allows gas only in a noncombustible room with power isolation (Fig. 2.4.3.1.1.1; §2.5.3). FM now allows its Approved water mist (HC-2), but wet pipe stays Arturo's life-safety choice.To validatethe battery kWh of a Vera Rubin rack (FM's rack rules stop at 20 kWh); the NFPA 855 edition, with the Cambridge Fire Department (Massachusetts enforces its fire code, 527 CMR 1.00, based on NFPA 1-2021, and Brookline's fire department still cites NFPA 855's 2020 edition); FM's DS 5-28 and DS 5-33 for the UPS and battery rooms; NFPA 2's full table for the reserved hydrogen pad.SourcesFM Global DS 5-32 (January 2026, interim revision July 2026) · NFPA 855 committee records (20 kWh per fire area, 600 kWh, NFPA 69) · UL on battery fire testing · Brookline Fire Department (NFPA 855, 2020) · NVIDIA's leak-detection levels and responses · Consulting-Specifying Engineer roundtable (June 2026)

budget.title: Purchase the fixed campus hardware
budget.why: Using the heavy reference reduces the number of people served for the same workload. It does not require purchasing a hypothetical fleet for all 400 million in this fixed-campus plan. The $30B five-year constraint still needs a complete cost review.
budget.html:
338 compute racks × $7.8M ≈ $2.64B per datacenter; six sites cost about $15.82B for compute-rack purchase only. This is not the earlier similarly numbered whole-project budget.

Networking, context memory, buildings, land, cooling, grid access, backup, electricity and operations are additional. The $30B five-year constraint has not been revalidated.

The previous $231–242B extrapolation purchased compute racks to chase the whole population under this same workload. It is not the fixed-campus purchase plan.

The old total-cost, leftover-budget, savings and payback headlines are superseded. Measure usage and finish the engineering estimate before making a financial commitment.

efficiency.title: Use the available electricity more effectively
efficiency.why: Efficient cooling supports more useful computation within the same electrical limit. This is a power comparison, not a new dollar-saving or payback claim.
efficiency.html:
For the same IT load, 1 − 1.10 ÷ 1.44 = 23.6% less facility power. At a fixed 500 MW, 500 ÷ 1.10 versus 500 ÷ 1.44 gives about 31% more power for IT.

Power is a rate; energy is power over time. One hour at the modeled 83.28 MW campus load uses 83.28 MWh. Actual daily and annual energy require an operating-load schedule, including idle demand.

The daily question and task counts stay fixed. The heavy model changes the chip time needed, while cooling, backup and boreholes still serve the same datacenter load.
efficiency.notes: SourceSupplied budget: PUE 1.10 design allowance versus large-site PUE 1.44. Daily and annual electricity require a load schedule; peak power is not an energy forecast.
